questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose UW, Seattle because I had previously visited the West Coast (Berkeley, California) and was interested in college-culture and loved the nature. Also, I wanted to attend a good university, but not on Lars tyndskids mark. I study psychology where we dont have a lot of electives, and UW also had the right courses for me, which is probably the real reason why I chose it :)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: KNOW that UW has quarters! I did fall+winter (october to late march), which doesnt allign well with the danish system. I struggeled a lot with coming home mid-march and starting school.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Not easy. You have to figure it out yourself, and KU cannot help you.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
None. If you have 'a major' (mine was psychology) you can speak to the advisers, they will tell you something about the programmes and help you. You have to contact them yourself.
If you live in the dorms (which I do not recommend) you will be in contact with volunteers, but they'll just hand you the key.

If you start in fall, there will be all kinds of activities, but they arent mandatory and there will be different people attending everything. The intro is mostly for freshmen, so as a 25 year old senior I felt pretty out of place.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: You will not be helped at UW, you need to do everything yourself. I was fine with it, but it's a steep learning curve.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: UW does housing through HFS, which is a private instutition. They have dorms with singles, doubles and triples. McMan has 'clusters' where you share kitchen and have common space, but its a very old building. Hansee has ok cheap singles. The other doms have common-spaces but these are not used by the college-kids (in my experience). I DO NOT RECOMMEND ON-CAMPUS HOUSING.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: MANDATORY mealplan, lowest mealplan is 1000$. I was in Madrona that had a kitchen, but without eqipment. It was rarely used. I was in a triple with two sweet 19-year olds, and I see myself as a very resilient person - but I hated it and ended up moving out. No sunlight, one ceiling light, anti-social, noisy hallways.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Think twice before you apply. I had to get out of my agreement after first quarter because I hated living in the dorms, and it was nearly impossible. They threatened to bill me for the whole 2nd quarter even though I didnt live there (5000$). I really think the food in the cafeteria was disgusting, but the on-campus supermarket was okay. Ate ramen and processed microwave food for 3 month, that was enough for me. 
Dorms are not social at UW, they are anti-social. I cannot describe how little I can recommend the dorms. Expensive, bad food, anti-social freshmen, HFS sucks.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I moved out of dorms after 1st quarter. It was okay to find an appartment. There are facebook-groups were sororities /senior houses are looking for roomies when they go on exchange. Expect to pay 800-1100 $ in rent. I would recommend future exchange students to find housing that way. You will meet nice college-students who are closer to your age, and more fun to live with than the freshmens in the dorms.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You get a date for your registration, and then your registration opens at 6am. Find your courses at
myplan.uw.edu
. 100 and 200 level courses are often work-load heavy because they are introduction courses. Expect to feel like you're in highschool but learn a lot!

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can contact your majors advisor (or any advisor really)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I got all the courses I wanted, but it was blood, sweat and tears. UW has tons of rules for who can register for what. You can easily get around prerequisites if you email the professor. Check your professor and your courses on
ratemyprofessor.com
. UW has so many courses, so you can spend ages looking at courses. If your professor doesn't answer or the advisers tell you that you can't register for a course, just go to the first class and talk to the professor. They have the final power, and most of them are so sweet and willing to help. Just remember to call them prof. xx and not their first name !

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
KU is not going to help you. Go talk to professors. You can apply for reduced course load on 2nd quarter. As a 25 year old, I really enjoyed talking graduate courses the most, because people were more similar to my age and the content was so much more interesting! It's more work, but if you want to get something out of your time on UW academically - I would say its your best bet :)
Also, take advantage of the possibility to enroll en all kinds of courses! I really enjoyed being able to choose so freely, and can recommend the gender studies and music department!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: 100-, 200- level are workload/deadline heavy and has final exams, where 300-, 400-, 500- have more reading but less deadlines. If you want an easy time (and prob a more interesting time) I suggest picking higher level courses. Also, then you won't be in class with 400 freshmen. I recommend the dinosaur class though! And the Marx course!

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As a psychology student, I was afraid that UW would have a very empirical/neuroscience/data-driven psychology program, because it's very competitive and that's what I heard about the US. Have been so pleasantly surprised! So many professors who do interesting personality-, social psychology research! They love if your interested in research, and will enroll you in their lab if your interested.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PSYCH 209 - Fundamentals of Psychological Research (not recommend)
MGMT 311 - Introduction to Strategic Human Resources Management
GWSS 500 - Social Feminist Theory (HIGHLY RECOMMEND)
MUSEN 300 - UW Symphony Orchestra

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer:
INFO 201 - Foundational Skills for Data Science (coding in R)
MUSIC 201 - 1st Year Music Theory
EDPLS 565 - Race, Equity, And Leading Educational Change
PSYCLN 531 - Developmental Psychopathology (HIGHLY RECOMMEND)
CONJ 570 - Clinical Management of Transgender Patients

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If your an psychology student, I would recommend looking into the first-year graduate program if you would like a bang for your buck academically. Professors and student are highly skilled, and are interested in the same critiques as we are having at home (aka alternative forelæsningsrække) and it meant a lot to me, that a top 10 US university were also having these conversations.

I also recommend prof Chandan Reddy if you're interested in feminism and neoliberalism and prof Eve Weinbaum if you're interested in marxism.

Lastly, UW has a notorious Computer Science program. Don't choose courses from that department unless you really want a steep learning curve.

I think future student should think about what they want from their exchange. It's difficult to not use a lot of time in school in the US, because there are so many deadlines.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I was surprised that on-campus housing was so expensive. Also comes without anything, so you have to buy pots and pans, linen, fridge, microwave - therefore I do not recommend it.

Also, you can easily waive the insurance at UW with your own travel-insurance.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Seattle is very expensive. Eating out is easily 20-30 dollars everywhere (but food on the Ave is really shitty, go somewhere else). Groceries are also expensive, but Trader Joes is okay. Get a friend who has a car or use Turo to rent cars fairly cheap for trips.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
UW has lots of clubs and RSOs. They are very difficult to find information about, so you really need to put in work. If you have something you're really good at (sport/music/etc), go to the audition! I was in the symphony orchestra and that was nice, but not very social and very elite.

Beginners have a harder time. Climbing club and hiking club do really cool trips, but it's harder to spark social connection because the clubs are so big. Find a niche club and go to meetings! The IMA (the sports center) has a lot of beginner sport, and you can take dance classes/yoga for 60$ a quarter.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I have been very disappointed in the social aspects of UWs exchange program. It's called CIRCLE and they do events. No one shows up and its awkward. Unite UW is a very intensive social program, some international students like it and I didn't do it so I won't be the judge - but it's a lot about telling stories and sharing insecurities, and it seemed a bit too intense for me - I suggest to go to the intro and see for yourself :)

As a danish student, you should apply for the Scandesign grant. They will invite you to events where you meet americans who went on exchange in DK - there I met some of my American friends. I mostly made friends in higher-level classes.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I recommend going on trips with the hiking/climbing club! The area around Seattle is amazing all time of year, and I've had the best experiences and met the nicest people in long early car-rides, doing long hikes, and climbing. Also, just rent cars with other exchange students and get out there! Seattle has three mountain ranges (Olympics, Cascades and Rainier) close, and all of them are stunning.

Twillight is filmed in Forks, and Twin Peaks is filmed in North Bend (the diner is still there!), Greys Anatomy and Ten Things I Hate About You is also from Seattle, so movie scene hunting!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Seatle has lot of good music venues

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Seattle is an interesting city. Used to be a little city known for grunge (Nirvana, Pearl Jam,
etc.etc
.), but is now a booming tech-city. It has grown a lot in the last 10 years, and gotten waaay more expensive. Big homelessness problem. Not as bad as San Fransisco, but very close. I'm a tough cookie, but I do not always feel safe on the streets. Choose Seattle because you can easily feel like you're a resident, a part of the city, and live in the middle of it - That would be too expensive in San Fransisco. Seattle is a smaller city than San Fransisco, and doesn't have the same 'big city feel'. It's more dirty than Vancouver, but to me also feels more authentic. Seattle has lots of good dive bars, and a lot of young people (most of them work for amazon though <3).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Be open to having friends than are younger than you :)

Seattle has a big scandinavian population, so tell them you're scandinavian and they will love you <3

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Living in the US, especially on the West Coast, you will be shocked about the homelessness. 

Seattle is expensive, so don't go if you don't feel like you have the funds. It's really no fun to be here if you're stressing about money and can't go on trips/go to concerts/etc.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Seattle has a lot of people moving in and out of the city - people are used to having friends for a short amount of time, and a lot of people are looking for friends(!) I have honestly found a lot of friends on Hinge and Feeld - it has been a good way to find people who were more my age, if I got a bit tired of college-kids and gave me a feeling of actually moving to another country and not 'just' being in an exchange program.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't live on campus
2. Talk to your professors
3. If you don't like the outdoors, you're going to be bored with Seattle.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
You can get Amazon Prime for free for 6 month as a UW student. Seattle public library is very good, and you can get free museum tickets. Ballard is cozy!
I loved having a bike and biking on the Burke Gilman Trail to Fremont and Ballard, North Seattle is young and cute!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
I did two weeks on the Pacific Crest Trail before starting school in October, and it was such an experience to be Pacific Northwest nature - I can really recommend doing Snoqualmie Pass to Stevens Pass!

After spending 6 month in Seattle, it is a city dear to my heart - but if you're used to living in Copenhagen, Seattle has some lacks city-wise. Everything closes early (5pm) and the culture-scene (museums, theaters, galleries) is quite lacking. But the mountains are beautiful!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Obviously moving across the world is challenging. There is a lot of practical stuff that will take a lot of your energy the first month. UW does not help you, so be sure to ask for help when you need it. Seek out other exchange students first. If you feel lonely, I garentee you that you're not the only one. Americans are very friendly, so get used to small-talking yourself through your day. A lot of people in Seattle are looking for friends, so just start conversation! 

In Seattle people come from all over the world, and I've found it surprisingly difficult to meet people from so diverse backgrounds - this means people are used to different ways of life and have different ideas of right and wrong. Stick to your values, and make sure to set boundaries (especially if you're dating)!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
